\title{Measuring Complex Tastes}

\author{Omar Lizardo\\ \small University of California, Los Angeles} \date{October 2026}

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\noindent This paper develops a geometric way to measure complex tastes, meaning cases in which what people like, do, and praise do not line up. Using a 2012 survey of 2,276 U.S. adults and twenty musical genres, we apply Multiple Factor Analysis to balance preference, consumption, and evaluation so no one aspect dominates the shared space. Preference and consumption are moderately related at the respondent level (RV = 0.35), while evaluation is nearly unrelated to both (RV = 0.01). The shared space has four interpretable dimensions, and the fourth is almost entirely an evaluation axis. Within individuals, aspect disagreement accounts for 49\% to 66\% of variation on each dimension. Demographics explain at most 10\% of the variation in total disagreement, and only 12 of the 96 coefficients across the four models survive a Holm correction.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Sociologists have measured cultural taste in at least three different ways \citep{ma2026tastes}. One tradition treats taste as \emph{preference}---a person's affective response to a cultural object. A second treats it as an orientation toward \emph{consumption}---actual participation or engagement in a cultural field. A third treats it as a faculty expressed in \emph{valuation}, through judgments about the quality or status of cultural objects. Rather than resolving this ambiguity by fiat, \citet{ma2026tastes} argues that taste should be understood pluralistically, as a person's ``thick subjectivity'' in a cultural field---a multidimensional orientation expressed through the multiple aspects of action that guide our preferences, engagement, and evaluations.

Taking taste's multiple aspects seriously sharpens the idea of \emph{complex taste}. In simple tastes, the aspects agree, so that what a person likes, does, and values all point the same way. In complex tastes they do not. The guilty pleasure (liked and consumed but not valued), the taste pose (liked and valued but not consumed), distanced consumption (consumed but neither liked nor valued), and their kin \citep{ma2026tastes} illustrate this.

This paper takes that pluralist conception seriously and builds a measurement strategy to match. The strategy applies Multiple Factor Analysis (MFA) \citep{pages2014mfa,abdi2013mfa}---a member of the Geometric Data Analysis (GDA) family that \citet{bourdieu1984distinction} used in his classic study \citep{rouanet2000geometric-a44, roux2004geometric-65c}---to a data structure in which each cultural object is described by three sets of indicators, one per each aspect of complex taste. MFA's block structure lets us ask the questions the theory of complex tastes raises directly, such as how strong are the links between preference, consumption, and evaluation? Do the three aspects contribute equally to the shared structure of taste? And what does the geometric signature of independent taste aspects look like when mapped to the same shared space?

The analysis is organized around four questions. Are preference, engagement, and evaluation empirically distinct, or do they index the same structure? Do the three aspects contribute equally to a shared space, and which dimensions does each one organize? How much do a person's aspects disagree, and does that disagreement follow social position? When genres rather than respondents are treated as the units, do some genres attract simpler tastes than others? Section~\ref{sec:data} describes the data and measures. The results come next, covering the shared space, individual disagreement, and its social and genre-level correlates. The discussion closes with the findings and their limits.

\section{Data and Measures}\label{sec:data}

\subsection{Data Source}

This analysis uses the Survey Sample International (SSI) 2012 Cultural Tastes Survey \citep{lizardo2012ssi},\footnote{The survey data and documentation are publicly available at \url{https://olizardo.github.io/SSI-2012/}.} a sample of $N = 2{,}276$ U.S. adults surveyed online in 2012. The data include no survey weights, and the analysis is unweighted, so the results describe this sample rather than the U.S. population. The survey asked respondents about their relationship to twenty musical genres, capturing how they feel about each genre, whether they engage with it, and how they perceive the people who enjoy it. After removing the 17 respondents with incomplete data on any of the 60 analysis variables, the working sample contains $N = 2{,}259$ respondents. The socio-demographic models in Section~\ref{sec:social} use the 2,258 of these respondents with no missing values on the demographic covariates (gender, race and ethnicity, age, education, parents' education, income, subjective class, and census region).

\subsection{Operationalizing the Three Aspects of Taste}

To measure complex tastes, we need distinct measures of preference, consumption, and evaluation for each genre. The survey collects data on all three, though operationalizing them as comparable binary indicators requires careful choices.

We operationalize preference as affective response by recoding the four-point liking scale (like, dislike, neither, or not familiar) into a binary. A respondent scores $1$ if they like the genre and $0$ otherwise. This treatment includes unfamiliar genres as non-preference, resting on the reasoning that affective preference requires at least knowing the object. You cannot prefer a genre you've never heard of. Consumption, by contrast, is straightforward. The survey asked respondents whether they had listened to each genre in the past month, a direct behavioral indicator coded $1$ for yes and $0$ for no. This gives a direct measure of engagement, independent of what people report liking. 

Evaluation poses the most difficult measurement challenge. To assess how respondents perceive the social status of each genre's fans, the survey asked them to mark a check-all-that-apply list of characteristics (college-educated, middle-class, upper-class, working-class, lower-class, and so on). But respondents often mark contradictory pairs, checking both ``college-educated'' and ``not college-educated,'' or both ``middle-class'' and ``working-class''---a pattern that reflects social ambiguity in how audiences are perceived. Yet for our analysis we need a single binary measure of high status attribution. We solve this by deeming a respondent to have high evaluation of a genre only when they signal \emph{unambiguous} high status. Specifically, a genre receives a $1$ if the respondent either checked college-educated \emph{without} checking not college-educated, \emph{or} checked middle or upper class \emph{without} checking working or lower class. This conservative standard requires respondents to avoid contradicting themselves, which makes evaluation the rarest of the three signals, as respondents attribute unambiguous high status to fewer genres than they like or listen to.

Table~\ref{tab:genre-rates} shows the prevalence of each coding. Overall, $41.7\%$ of genre-responses are coded $1$ on preference, $22.9\%$ on consumption, and $20.7\%$ on evaluation. Prevalence falls from preference to evaluation. Respondents like more genres than they listen to, and listen to more than they credit with high status. The unambiguous-status standard is demanding, requiring explicit social positioning without internal contradiction, so evaluation becomes the least frequently affirmed aspect of taste.

\section{Mapping the Space of Complex Tastes}

As we have seen, our data gives us three separate pictures of each person's taste. These show what they like, what they listen to, and what they think about the people who do. These three pictures might overlap heavily (a person who likes opera probably listens to it and sees its fans as high status), or they might diverge (someone might listen to hip-hop while considering it low status and claiming not to like it). To answer our core questions---how much do these three pictures agree, do they contribute equally to a single coherent picture, and where do people end up when their pictures don't line up---we use Multiple Factor Analysis (MFA) \citep{pages2014mfa,abdi2013mfa}. This method takes data organized into distinct blocks of variables (here, the three aspects of taste) and builds a single shared picture of respondents while ensuring no one block dominates. We use \emph{blocks of variables}, or \emph{aspects} when referring specifically to preference, engagement, and evaluation, reserving ``group'' for its ordinary sociological meaning.

\subsection{The Global Structure of Taste and the Compromise Space}
\label{sec:mfa}

The raw data is a table with one row per respondent and sixty columns, twenty genres each measured on three aspects. Each entry is binary, containing a 1 if the person likes/listens to/evaluates the genre highly, and 0 otherwise. To construct the global space that combines preferences, consumption, and evaluations, we proceed in two steps. 

In the first step, we run a separate analysis on just the liking data (20 genres, 2,259 respondents), treating it as a two-way table of yes/no responses. This analysis shows how respondents cluster by what they like. We repeat the process independently for listening and for evaluations. In GDA terms, each of these is a Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA) on one block of twenty binary variables and the same number of individuals. MCA is a method designed for categorical data that positions respondents and categories in a shared space according to their yes/no patterns, in much the way that standard correlations or principal components work for continuous data \citep{roux2004geometric-65c, pages2014mfa}. The result of each separate MCA is a map of the respondents, showing who is similar to whom in terms of liking alone, listening alone, or evaluations alone.

After the first step, the next task is to merge these three separate pictures into one. But we face a problem here because if one aspect naturally has stronger patterns than another (if listening, say, reveals sharper clustering than evaluations), it will dominate the combined picture. To prevent this, before merging, we weight each aspect inversely to the magnitude of the eigenvalue corresponding to the first dimension of the separate MCA we just described \citep{pages2014mfa}. The first dimension of the MCA for preference had an eigenvalue of $0.1550$; for consumption, $0.1265$; for evaluation, $0.1942$. The aspect with the largest eigenvalue ($\lambda_1$) has the strongest patterns, so we downweight it by using the weight $1/\lambda_1$. That gives weights of $6.45$ for preference ($1/0.1550$), $7.90$ for consumption ($1/0.1265$), and $5.15$ for evaluation ($1/0.1942$). 

We apply the weights in three steps. First, we expand each aspect's indicators into yes/no columns for each genre (the MCA indicator matrix), doubling the columns from 20 to 40. We center each column at its mean $m_c$ and divide by $\sqrt{m_c(1-m_c)}$. Each column is then multiplied by $\sqrt{(1-m_c)/(\lambda_{1,h} J)}$, where $J = 20$ is the number of genre variables in the aspect, each of which contributes two columns. Together, these two steps give each column the weight $1/m_c$ (up to a constant) in the distances between respondents, so a rare answer counts most whether it is yes or no. This also carries the aspect's balancing weight $1/\lambda_{1,h}$, so that each block is scaled by $1/\sqrt{\lambda_{1,h}}$. We then concatenate the three weighted matrices column-wise (creating a matrix of dimensions $N \times 120$, where $N$ is the number of individuals) and run a principal components analysis (PCA) on the combined table. The PCA yields individual and column scores across multiple dimensions that define the shared compromise space. The result is a ``complex taste space''---a single map of respondents in which the three aspects carry equal weight.\footnote{Respondents who give a constant answer within an aspect---liking all twenty genres or none, listening to all or none, granting unambiguous high status to the fans of all twenty genres or of none ($N = 412$, mostly the $321$ who grant status to no genre)---are treated as supplementary individuals, projected onto the space rather than contributing to its construction. They are excluded from the active subsample ($N = 1{,}847$) because constancy within a block is a nonresponse pattern, not a substantive taste position; respondents constant in one block typically vary in others. As a robustness check, we re-estimated the MFA treating them as active and the previous fit as supplementary; the substantive results are unchanged---the same four dimensions reappear in matched pairs (correlations between matched-dimension coordinates across the two fits range from $0.87$ to $0.97$), with similar eigenvalues and RV coefficients. We also re-estimated the same MFA with each separate block analyzed by scaled PCA instead of MCA; eigenvalues and RV coefficients are nearly identical and individual coordinates correlate at $r$ between $0.82$ and $0.99$ across the four dimensions. The main difference is how MCA up-weights rare categories. MCA emphasizes rare (distinctive) answers, a feature we want here since unusual taste patterns carry theoretical interest.}

\subsubsection{Are the Three Aspects Empirically Distinct?}

Before interpreting what the resulting dimensions reveal, we must establish whether the three aspects are separate measures or different angles on the same underlying structure. The RV coefficient, the multivariate analog of a correlation, answers this question. It compares the respondent-similarity matrices of the two aspects and measures how closely they line up, as Equation~\ref{eq:rv} shows.

\begin{equation}
\mathrm{RV}(h,k) = \frac{\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_h \mathbf{S}_k)}{\sqrt{\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_h^2)\,\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_k^2)}}.
\label{eq:rv}
\end{equation}

Here, $\mathbf{S}_h$ is the respondent-similarity matrix for aspect $h$,\footnote{Formally, $\mathbf{S}_h = \mathbf{X}_h \mathbf{D}_h \mathbf{X}_h^\mathsf{T}$, an $N \times N$ matrix. Here $\mathbf{X}_h$ is the $N \times 2J$ indicator matrix for aspect $h$, with a yes and a no column for each of the $J = 20$ genres. Each column $c$ is centered at its mean $m_c$ and divided by $\sqrt{m_c(1-m_c)}$, and $\mathbf{D}_h$ is diagonal with entries $(1-m_c)/(\lambda_{1,h} J)$, where $\lambda_{1,h}$ is the first eigenvalue of the separate analysis of aspect $h$. Each entry $S_{h,ij}$ therefore measures the weighted overlap in the indicator patterns of respondents $i$ and $j$ across the twenty genres.} capturing pairwise respondent similarities based on that aspect's twenty genres. RV ranges from 0 to 1. It equals 1 only when one aspect's similarity matrix is a constant multiple of the other's, and it falls toward 0 as the two matrices become nearly orthogonal, so that one aspect's pattern of respondent similarities says almost nothing about the other's.

Table~\ref{tab:rv} lists all pairwise RV values, along with each aspect's RV with the MFA compromise (0.72, 0.77, and 0.43 for preference, consumption, and evaluation). For preference and consumption, we find RV = 0.35, which indicates moderate similarity but far from identity. Respondents who are similar in their liking patterns tend to be similar in their listening patterns, but the pattern of pairwise similarities differs between the two aspects. One respondent might be a heavy engager with moderate discriminating taste, while another is an intense discriminator who listens rarely.\footnote{We conducted all analyses in \textsf{R} using the \textsf{FactoMineR} package \citep{le2008factominer}; scripts reproducing all results are available at \url{https://github.com/olizardo/measuring-complex-tastes}.} Evaluation tells quite a different story. It shows an RV of $0.014$ with preference and $0.015$ with consumption---near-zero values that are central to the argument. The evaluation similarity structure is nearly unrelated to the liking and listening structures. Knowing whether someone likes many genres tells you little about whether they grant high status to those genres' fans. The three aspects of complex tastes are thus empirically distinct. What you like, what you listen to, and what you praise are three partially separable dimensions of taste. This independence is why complex tastes can exist geometrically. A person can like a genre without listening to it, listen without liking, or evaluate highly without doing either.

\subsubsection{The Four Dimensions of Taste}

The global space resulting from the MFA analysis described in section~\ref{sec:mfa} organizes respondents along four interpretable dimensions, each capturing a distinct structure in how preferences, engagement, and evaluations align or diverge. Table~\ref{tab:eigen} shows that the first dimension captures $8.23\%$ of the variation, the second $7.25\%$, the third $5.39\%$, the fourth $5.11\%$, and the first five dimensions together $30.35\%$.\footnote{These percentages are typical for data like ours---binary yes/no responses scattered across twenty genres analyzed via MCA. Much of the variation is genre-specific (whether you like opera has little to do with whether you like hip-hop), so no single dimension captures huge amounts.} In the GDA tradition, this variation is called \emph{inertia}---the total spread or dispersion of the respondent cloud around its center. When we say a dimension captures $8.23\%$ of the inertia, we mean that ordering respondents along that dimension explains $8.23\%$ of how different they are from one another in their sixty-dimensional response pattern.

To understand what each dimension means, we examine where the twenty genres land in the space. For each genre and aspect, the MFA assigns a position along each dimension based on respondents' patterns; genres with many "yes" answers sit where respondents who gave those answers cluster, while genres with few "yes" answers sit where their rare endorsers sit. These positions, shown in Figure~\ref{fig:categories1-2} and~\ref{fig:categories3-4}, reveal the structure each dimension captures. 

On the first dimension, preference and consumption place genres cleanly along the traditional prestige hierarchy. The consecrated genres sit on the positive side (opera at $+0.72$ for consumption and $+0.61$ for preference; classical at $+0.64$ for consumption; big band at $+0.69$ for consumption), while the popular genres sit on the negative side (rap/hip-hop at $-1.26$ for consumption and indie rock at $-1.29$ for consumption). Whether we measure liking or listening, the same genres cluster together---the classic \emph{highbrow--popular hierarchy} that researchers have documented for decades \citep{bourdieu1984distinction,jæger2024from-a4b}. The hierarchy is linked to generation \citep{lizardo2015musical-8c6}, with older people tending toward the highbrow pole and younger people toward the popular pole, a result we discuss in Section~\ref{sec:social}. Status attributions, by contrast, barely move along this dimension (their genre positions range from $-0.23$ for rap/hip-hop to $+0.39$ for dance/club music). Dimension 1 is thus a \emph{highbrow--popular} axis.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig-categories-d12} \caption{Category map of the MFA (dimensions 1--2). Colored labels mark the ``yes'' categories of each aspect; grey points are the corresponding ``no'' categories. On Dimension 1 the preference and consumption ``yes'' categories split highbrow (right) from popular (left); on Dimension 2 (volume) all of them sit on the positive side, the rarest engagements furthest from the origin. On Dimension 3 (engagement divide) the diaspora genres sit positive and the guitar-rock cluster sits negative. Evaluation ``yes'' categories barely spread on these three axes.}
\label{fig:categories1-2}
\end{figure}

Dimension 2 is a \emph{volume} axis, ordered by how much respondents engage at all. Every preference and consumption yes category sits on the positive side, and the rarer the engagement, the further out the category sits. Listening to folk ($+1.35$), bluegrass ($+1.31$), or big band ($+1.19$) places a respondent far along the axis, while listening to rap/hip-hop ($+0.05$) or heavy metal ($+0.03$) barely moves it, because those engagements are widespread. Liking follows the same rarity ordering (folk at $+0.84$, big band at $+0.80$, opera at $+0.78$ at the extremes). Evaluation yes categories follow rarity as well---granting status to blues/R\&B fans ($+0.59$), Latin/salsa fans ($+0.57$), or heavy metal fans ($+0.51$) is more distinctive than granting it to classical music fans ($+0.03$)---but they stay far closer to the origin than the engagement categories. Where respondents sit on this axis thus depends on the sheer volume of their engagement.

As Figure~\ref{fig:categories3-4} shows, dimension 3 separates the preference and consumption categories of non-highbrow genres by broad ``music world'' type rather than by prestige \citep{silver2022balancing-5a8}. The consumption yes categories for the Black, Latin, and Caribbean diaspora genres sit at the positive pole---reggae at $+0.95$, Latin/salsa at $+0.76$, rap/hip-hop at $+0.61$---while the guitar-rock cluster sits at the negative pole (heavy metal at $-0.91$, indie rock at $-0.76$). Liking mirrors the same contrast (rap/hip-hop at $+0.60$, Latin/salsa at $+0.51$, reggae at $+0.45$, against heavy metal at $-0.62$ and indie rock at $-0.53$), while evaluation is nearly silent (its yes categories span only $-0.33$ to $+0.17$). Where respondents sit on this dimension depends on which genres they engage with, and the dimension is linked to race and ethnicity (Section~\ref{sec:social}).

The vertical axis of the category map in Figure~\ref{fig:categories3-4} (Dimension 4) tells a different story. All twenty evaluation yes categories sit clustered on the positive side of the origin. The preference and consumption yes categories, by contrast, scatter around zero. On this dimension, the rarer the high-status attribution for a genre, the higher that genre sits (rap/hip-hop and Latin/salsa at $+1.94$, against $+0.02$ for classical music and $+0.00$ for opera)---popular genres receive high-status attributions from fewer respondents, making their fans appear as distinctive high-status recipients. This is the \emph{status-valuation} dimension, almost entirely an evaluation axis. A respondent's position here depends almost solely on how they distribute status recognition across genres' fans, independent of their liking or listening. Generous respondents---those who grant high status to fans of most genres---sit high on the vertical axis, while respondents who reserve high status for traditionally consecrated genres (like classical or opera) sit low.

\subsection{Relationships Between the Three Aspects}

Now that we have verified the aspects are distinct and seen what each dimension captures, we can ask two more questions. Do all three aspects contribute equally to the global space, and do they dominate different dimensions?

\subsubsection{Participation and the Lg Coefficient}

Given that the aspects are partially independent, a second question arises. When we merge them into one compromise space, do all three actually show up, or does one get swallowed by the others? The Lg coefficient measures how much of each aspect's internal structure survives this merging process. It assesses the inner product of each aspect's configuration matrix with the combined MFA, as Equation~\ref{eq:lg} shows.

\begin{equation}
Lg(h, \mathrm{MFA}) = \frac{1}{\lambda_1^{\mathrm{MFA}}} \sum_{k=1}^{H} \frac{\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_h \mathbf{S}_k)}{N^2}.
\label{eq:lg}
\end{equation}

Here, $\mathbf{S}_h$ and $\mathbf{S}_k$ are the respondent-similarity matrices for aspects $h$ and $k$ (defined in the previous section; the balancing weight $1/\lambda_{1,h}$ is already built into $\mathbf{S}_h$), $N$ is the number of respondents, $H = 3$ is the number of aspects, and $\lambda_1^{\mathrm{MFA}}$ is the first eigenvalue of the global MFA. The sum over $k$ includes $k = h$. In plain terms, $Lg(h, \mathrm{MFA})$ measures how much of aspect $h$'s internal structure---the pattern of which respondents are similar to which others based on that aspect---is preserved in the compromise space. If an aspect's structure is completely lost in the merge, $Lg$ is near zero; if it survives intact, $Lg$ is high. The coefficient is not bounded above, and its magnitude reflects both how much structure an aspect brings to the merge and how much of that structure the compromise carries. 

Table~\ref{tab:groups} shows the estimated $Lg$ coefficients from the MFA analysis. Preference contributes 2.73, consumption 3.34, and evaluation 1.30. Consumption shares the most structure with the compromise and preference is close behind, while evaluation contributes the least---the same pattern the RV coefficients revealed. The shortfall for evaluation reflects its near-independence from the liking and listening patterns that dominate the first three dimensions; evaluation concentrates its participation on Dimension 4. Each aspect still contributes to the compromise space, although the contributions are unequal.

\subsubsection{Aspect Contributions to Each Dimension}

Equal overall participation masks asymmetries. The three aspects do not dominate equally on every dimension. Some dimensions are shaped primarily by liking or listening, while others belong to evaluation. Each category's contribution to a dimension is its share of that dimension's inertia. Within an aspect, it is proportional to the category's mass $p_j$ times its squared coordinate $f_{js}^2$. The contribution of aspect $h$ to dimension $s$ is the sum over the yes and no categories of its twenty genres, as Equation~\ref{eq:ctr} shows.

\begin{equation}
\mathrm{Ctr}(h,s) = \sum_{j \in h} \mathrm{ctr}_{js}.
\label{eq:ctr}
\end{equation}

Within each aspect, the category contribution takes the form in Equation~\ref{eq:ctrcat}
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{ctr}_{js} = \frac{100\, p_j f_{js}^2}{J\,\lambda_{1,h}\,\lambda_s^2},
\label{eq:ctrcat}
\end{equation}
where $\mathrm{ctr}_{js}$ is the contribution of category $j$ to dimension $s$, $p_j$ is that category's mass (its share of respondents), $f_{js}$ is its coordinate on dimension $s$, $J = 20$ is the number of genres, $\lambda_{1,h}$ is aspect $h$'s balancing eigenvalue, and the sum over $j \in h$ runs over the $2J = 40$ yes and no categories of aspect $h$. By construction, contributions sum to $100\%$ across all categories of the three aspects on each dimension. 

Table~\ref{tab:groups} shows the resulting aspect contributions to each dimension. On Dimensions 1--3, the distribution of contributions is relatively flat, with consumption dominating Dimension 1 at 54.6\%, preference leading Dimension 2 at 52.3\%, and consumption again leading Dimension 3 at 56.3\%. Across the first three dimensions, evaluation contributes only 1.1\%, 4.2\%, and 3.1\% respectively. Preference and consumption pull in the same direction---the genre hierarchy and the intensity of engagement show up in both aspects' structures---even though the separate analyses order their internal axes differently. As we can see, Dimension 4 inverts this picture. Evaluation accounts for 91.1\%, with preference and consumption contributing 4.3\% and 4.6\%. The first evaluation axis correlates 0.95 with Dimension 4 (Table~\ref{tab:partial-axes}). What you like and listen to tells you little about how you distribute status attributions. Evaluation follows a pattern of its own, only loosely connected to preference and consumption. Dimension 4 is where that separation shows most clearly.

\subsection{Measuring How Much Individual Tastes Come Apart}

So far we've asked about the space as a whole. How independent are the aspects? Do all three participate? Which aspect participates the most on which dimension? Now we flip back to the individual level and ask \emph{For each person, on each dimension, how much do their three aspects agree or disagree?}

\subsubsection{Agreement and Disagreement Between Aspects}

To measure within-person disagreement, we proceed as follows. First, note that each person has \textit{three} separate coordinates on each Dimension---one from the separate MCA analyses of their preferences, one from the consumption analysis, plus a third one based on their evaluations---one per aspect. For Dimension 1, let us call these $F_{1,\text{p}}$, $F_{1,\text{c}}$, $F_{1,\text{e}}$. These three aspect-specific coordinates are called that person's three \emph{partial points} on the specified dimension of the compromise space. The partial points are computed with each aspect's balancing weight (the inverse of its first eigenvalue) built into the metric, so that they are expressed in the global MFA coordinate system. The global position is the average of these three partial points, which makes it the geometric center of the aspect-specific positions. Now all three of these points may be very close (and even coincide); alternatively, the three might not be very close. For instance, Person A might have all three coordinates at $+2$ (perfect agreement). Person B might have coordinates at $+3$, $+1$, and $-1$ (large disagreement).

We measure this disagreement with a score called $W_s(i)$. This score answers the question of how much person $i$'s three aspects disagree on dimension $s$. If all three dimension-specific scores are identical, $W_s(i) = 0$ (simple taste, complete agreement). If they're far apart, $W_s(i)$ is large (complex taste, large disagreement).

Equation~\ref{eq:decomp} gives the decomposition, which holds exactly.

\begin{equation}
\sum_{h=1}^{H} F_{sh}(i)^2 \;=\; H \cdot F_s(i)^2 \;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{h=1}^{H} \left(F_{sh}(i) - F_s(i)\right)^2}_{W_s(i)},
\label{eq:decomp}
\end{equation}

Where $F_{sh}(i)$ is person $i$'s coordinate on dimension $s$ for aspect $h$ (the partial point), $F_s(i)$ is the person's global position on dimension $s$ (the average of the three aspect-specific coordinates), $W_s(i)$ is the disagreement score, and $H = 3$ the number of aspects being considered. The first term ($H \cdot F_s(i)^2$) measures how far from the center all three aspects place them together---their shared position. The second term ($W_s(i)$) measures the sum of squared deviations of each aspect's position from the mean, telling us how much the three aspects pull in different directions. Scaling up from individuals to the full sample takes one more step. For each respondent, the share of their dimension-$s$ variation attributable to disagreement is $W_s(i)/T_s(i)$, where $T_s(i) = H \cdot F_s(i)^2 + W_s(i)$ is their total variation on that dimension---shared position plus disagreement. Averaging this share across respondents yields the dimension-level disagreement shares reported below. Because the disagreement share and the position share (the rest of each respondent's variation, which comes from where they sit when all their aspects point the same direction, the shared consensus position) sum to one for every respondent, their averages do too.\footnote{The ratio of summed inertias, $\sum_i W_s(i) / \sum_i \sum_h F_{sh}(i)^2$, gives a similar aggregate decomposition with somewhat smaller disagreement shares.}

To make this concrete, consider two respondents (362 and 1881), plotted together in the global space in Figure~\ref{fig:worked-example}. One likes fifteen of the twenty genres---from jazz, classic rock/oldies, and country to top 40 and heavy metal---listens to nine of them, and credits the fans of eighteen genres with unambiguously high status (a somewhat ecumenical picture of the status of genres). The other likes fourteen genres, listens to thirteen, and grants high status to none---a stance of withholding evaluation despite high engagement. Both are heavy engagers, with global volume coordinates near $+3$, yet they differ in how their three aspects align. 

On the \emph{highbrow--popular dimension} (left panel, horizontal axis), both respondents disagree more than most of the sample, with $W_1 = 7.0$ for the first and $W_1 = 9.6$ for the second, placing them at the 88th and 94th percentiles (the sample median is 2.2). The aspects that drive this disagreement differ, however. For the first respondent, preference sits well down the popular side ($-2.61$) while consumption and evaluation sit slightly on the highbrow side ($+0.61$ and $+0.66$), around a global point of $-0.45$; the squared distance of the preference point from that global position accounts for about two-thirds of $W_1$. For the second respondent, consumption sits well up the highbrow side ($+3.34$) while preference ($-0.65$) and evaluation ($-0.23$) sit slightly below center, averaging to a global point of $+0.82$; here the consumption point accounts for about two-thirds of $W_1$. In both cases one aspect pulls away from the other two, but it is a different aspect in each case. 

On the \emph{volume dimension} (right panel's horizontal axis), the first respondent's three aspect points cluster tightly ($+3.07$, $+3.41$, and $+2.90$), giving $W_2 = 0.13$, close to zero. The second respondent's consumption point sits far above their preference and evaluation points ($+7.82$ against $+3.39$ and $-0.70$), yielding $W_2 = 36.29$, above the 99th percentile. The difference lies in the fourth dimension (the vertical axis of both panels). The first respondent's evaluation point rises ($+14.42$) while preference and consumption sit slightly below zero ($-0.76$ and $-0.96$), creating $W_4 = 155.7$; the second's three points all sit on the withholding side ($-0.47$, $-2.35$, and $-2.65$) around a global point of $-1.82$, yielding minimal $W_4 = 2.8$. The same high engagement produces disagreement on different dimensions. Respondent 362's complexity stems from evaluating generously while engaging selectively, and respondent 1881's stems from withholding evaluation while engaging widely.

\begin{figure}[htbp!]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig-worked-example} \caption{\footnotesize Worked example. Partial points of two contrasting respondents plotted in the same space, on the plane spanned by the highbrow--popular axis (Dimension 1, left panel) and the volume axis (Dimension 2, right panel) with the status-valuation axis (Dimension 4, vertical in both). Colors distinguish the respondents (blue = grants high status to 18 of 20 genres, orange = grants high status to none); shapes mark the aspects (circle = preference, triangle = consumption, square = evaluation, drawn hollow for the orange respondent so that coincident points remain visible); diamonds are each respondent's global (compromise) position, the average of their three partial points, and solid segments connect each partial point to it. Plotting both respondents in a common space makes their separation visible---nearly the same position on the volume dimension (right panel), opposite sides of zero on the status-valuation axis. On the left panel, the first respondent's preference partial sits on the popular side while the other two sit slightly on the highbrow side ($W_1 = 7.0$, 92\% of their variation on this dimension), and the second respondent's consumption partial sits well up the highbrow side ($W_1 = 9.6$, 83\%). The generous respondent's evaluation partial rises up the status-valuation axis while their preference and consumption partials stay near zero, so their aspects disagree about status ($W_4 = 155.7$, 74\% of their variation on this dimension); the withholding respondent's three partials bunch below zero ($W_4 = 2.8$, 22\%)---a difference of more than fifty-fold.}
\label{fig:worked-example}
\end{figure}

Across the sample, how much of a person's own variation on each dimension comes from their aspects disagreeing, and how much from where they sit when their aspects agree? Averaging each respondent's disagreement share $W_s(i)/T_s(i)$ across the sample answers this. On Dimension 1 the average disagreement share is 49\%, leaving 51\% for global position. On Dimension 2 it is 55\% against 45\%, on Dimension 3 52\% against 48\%, and on Dimension 4 66\% against 34\%. Aspect disagreement is roughly as important as where respondents sit when their aspects agree (their global position) in shaping the structure of the space. Complex tastes are not confined to a few unusual respondents. They appear throughout the structure of the space.

\subsubsection{Pairwise Disagreements and Sources of Complexity}

The overall score $W_s(i)$ does not say which two aspects are pulling apart. Each pair of aspects defines a squared distance on each dimension, and these distances sum to $H \cdot W_s(i)$, so they partition the total disagreement among the pairs, as Equation~\ref{eq:pairwise} states.

\begin{equation}
\sum_{h<k} \left(F_{sh}(i) - F_{sk}(i)\right)^2 = H \cdot W_s(i)
\label{eq:pairwise}
\end{equation}

Here $F_{sh}(i)$ is respondent $i$'s partial point for aspect $h$ on dimension $s$, and the sum runs over the three pairs of aspects. The identity holds because, for any $H$ numbers, the sum of squared pairwise differences equals $H$ times the sum of squared deviations from their mean.

Table~\ref{tab:pairs} reports the sample mean of each pairwise distance on each dimension, together with each pair's average share of the respondent's dimension total. For a given respondent, a pair's share is its squared distance divided by the sum of the three pairwise distances on that dimension, which equals $H \cdot W_s(i)$. The table's percentages average these shares across respondents, so each respondent contributes equally regardless of how much disagreement they have. Dimension 4 is the most concentrated case. The preference--evaluation and consumption--evaluation pairs each average about 46\% of a respondent's Dimension 4 total, and the preference--consumption pair averages 9\%. Evaluations therefore sit apart from liking and listening on this dimension. On the other dimensions the split is more even. The consumption--evaluation pair has the largest average share on Dimension 1 (42\%) and Dimension 3 (40\%), and the preference--evaluation pair on Dimension 2 (38\%).

The bottom row, $H$ times the mean of $W_s$, equals the sum of the three pair means.}

\subsubsection{Genre-Based and Cross-Genre Sources of Complexity}

The score $W_s(i)$ can also be split by \emph{where} the disagreement originates. A respondent might hold contradictory opinions of a single genre---liking it but not valuing it highly, for instance---or the same kind of disagreement might repeat across many genres and reinforce itself, or cancel out. Respondents with the same total $W_s(i)$ can arrive there through either pattern. Some arrive through intense within-genre contradictions, and others through consistent contradiction across the whole repertoire. The following decomposition separates these two sources.

\begin{equation}
W_s(i) \;=\; \underbrace{\sum_{g=1}^{G} H^2 \sum_{h=1}^{H} d_{ighs}^2}_{\substack{\omega_s(i;g) \\ \text{genre-based}}} \;+\; \underbrace{2H^2 \sum_{g < g'} \sum_{h=1}^{H} d_{ighs} d_{ig'hs}}_{\substack{\gamma_s(i) \\ \text{coherence}}}
\label{eq:genre}
\end{equation}

The first term, $\sum_g \omega_s(i;g)$, captures the respondent's \emph{genre-based complex taste}---how much their three aspects contradict each other within specific individual genres. For each genre $g$, we measure deviations $d_{ighs} = c_{ihs} - \bar{c}_{ghs}$, where $c_{ihs}$ is respondent $i$'s partial point for aspect $h$ on dimension $s$, and $\bar{c}_{ghs}$ is the mean of all respondents' partial points for aspect $h$ on that genre (this is the genre's category score from the global MFA). For example, suppose genre $g$ has an average position of $0$ on dimension $s$ across all respondents. If this respondent's preference partial sits at $+2$, consumption at $-1$, and evaluation at $+3$, the three deviations are $+2$, $-1$, and $+3$; their squared sum makes $\omega_s(i;g)$ large for that genre. Summed across all twenty genres, $\sum_g \omega_s(i;g)$ captures total genre-based disagreement. This component is especially large when a respondent's three aspects contradict each other within specific genres---when a person likes a genre but doesn't value it (a guilty pleasure), or values it without listening to it (distant praise).

The second term, $\gamma_s(i)$, captures \emph{cross-genre coherence}---whether a respondent's per-genre deviations $d_{ighs}$ point in the same direction across different genres (reinforcing disagreement) or in opposite directions (cancelling disagreement). It measures whether the pattern of disagreement within a respondent is consistent or contradictory across genres. Formally, it sums the products of deviations for each pair of genres, within each aspect. If a respondent deviates positively for genre $g$ and negatively for genre $g'$ on the same aspect, the product is negative and reduces total disagreement. If the deviations both point the same way across genres, the product is positive and increases it. Positive $\gamma_s(i)$ means the respondent's per-genre disagreements reinforce each other across genres; negative $\gamma_s(i)$ means they cancel out.

Returning to our first respondent from the highbrow--popular example, the contrast comes on the \emph{status-valuation axis} (vertical, Dimension 4). Their preference and consumption points sit slightly on the withholding side of the origin ($-0.76$ and $-0.96$), while the evaluation point lies far out on the generous side ($+14.42$), since they grant high status to nearly every genre's fans. The global point is $+4.24$, and the disagreement is large. The total is $W_4 = (-0.76 - 4.24)^2 + (-0.96 - 4.24)^2 + (14.42 - 4.24)^2 = 155.7$, 93\% of which is cross-genre coherence ($\gamma_4 = 144.4$). Nearly everything that places this respondent on the status-valuation dimension is disagreement between aspects. The second respondent's three points all sit on the withholding side ($-0.47$, $-2.35$, and $-2.65$ for preference, consumption, and evaluation), around a global point of $-1.82$. Their $W_4 = 2.8$ (22\% of their variation on this dimension) reflects mild geometry due to small coordinates throughout. Thus, despite their opposite evaluation patterns, both respondents are heavy engagers (similar positions on the volume dimension), yet their status-valuation disagreement differs by a factor of more than fifty. The first is complex on the status-valuation dimension alone; the second on the volume dimension alone.

The total $W_s(i)$ can also be reached through different mixes of the two components. For the first respondent above, nearly all of $W_4 = 155.7$ is cross-genre coherence ($\gamma_4 = 144.4$, against $\omega_4 = 11.2$). The same kind of contradiction recurs across the repertoire and reinforces itself. A respondent with a similar total could instead get most of it from a handful of genres where liking and valuing pull apart, with little repetition across genres. A third pattern runs the other way. Contradictions in one direction can be offset by opposite contradictions elsewhere, so the coherence term is negative and the total is smaller than the genre-level parts would suggest. Identical totals can therefore hide different underlying structures, which is why the decomposition is reported alongside $W_s(i)$.

Appendix~\ref{app:comparison} compares the geometric and configuration-count measures of complex tastes.

\subsection{The Socio-Demographic Correlates of Complex Tastes}
\label{sec:social}

We ask \emph{who has complex tastes?} We know taste positions are socially stratified---older people like highbrow music, younger people popular, and so forth \citep{bourdieu1984distinction,bennett2009culture-aef}. But are people who experience disagreement between their aspects concentrated in particular demographic groups, or scattered throughout?

Total disagreement is only weakly patterned by demographics. When we model the disagreement scores $W_s(i)$ using demographics, we find that age, education, income, race, class, gender, parents' education, and region together explain only $4.4\%$ of the variation in $W_1$ (highbrow--popular), $3.6\%$ in $W_2$ (volume), $10.0\%$ in $W_3$ (engagement divide), and $1.9\%$ in $W_4$ (status valuation). A model with 24 coefficients would explain about one percent of the variation by chance, so these fits are modest but not zero, and the individual coefficients carry most of the substantive content. 

Taste position on the genre hierarchy has a long record of social patterning \citep{lizardo2015musical-8c6}. Whether aspect disagreement follows the same pattern is an open question, and the answer here is mixed. A few contrasts are large and survive correction, while most are small.

Table~\ref{tab:regression} reports the 96 coefficients of the four models with 95\% confidence intervals. Unadjusted, 26 have $p < .05$, and 12 remain significant under a Holm correction across the table (marked with $^{\dagger}$). The remaining coefficients are treated as exploratory. On the highbrow--popular axis ($W_1$), disagreement falls with age from the thirties through the sixties. The 50--59 coefficient is $-1.65$ (95\% CI $-2.12$ to $-1.18$), and the 60--69 coefficient is $-1.59$, so these two groups cannot be distinguished. The South's lower disagreement relative to the Northeast ($b = -0.42$, $p = .04$) does not survive correction. On the volume dimension ($W_2$), upper-class respondents show more disagreement ($b = 4.54$, $p < .001$), as do those with college-educated parents ($b = 1.52$, $p < .001$). On the engagement-divide dimension ($W_3$), racial and ethnic differences are visible. Black respondents show more disagreement ($b = 1.61$, $p < .001$), as do those identifying with multiple races ($b = 1.41$, $p < .001$) and Hispanic respondents ($b = 0.52$, $p < .001$), while those 60 and older show less disagreement ($b = -0.77$ and $-0.93$, both $p < .001$). On the status-valuation dimension ($W_4$), upper-class respondents show more disagreement ($b = 9.16$, 95\% CI $4.0$ to $14.3$). This is the largest coefficient in the table, and it survives correction only narrowly ($p = .04$). Every age group above 18--29 has a positive coefficient between $1.8$ and $2.6$, but the intervals run from roughly $-0.5$ to about $5$, and none survives correction.\footnote{In the log-outcome models, the upper-class coefficients on $W_2$ ($\beta = 0.54$, $p = .007$) and $W_4$ ($\beta = 0.74$, $p = .002$) remain, corresponding to roughly 70\% and 110\% higher disagreement. The age coefficients on $W_4$ do not. Ages 30--39 give $\beta = 0.20$ ($p = .06$), and ages 40--49 give $\beta = 0.03$ ($p = .80$). On $W_1$, the log model shows the age decline through the sixties but a positive coefficient for ages 70+ ($\beta = 0.26$, $p = .01$), so the age gradient should not be described as monotone.} Unadjusted, Hispanic identity ($b = 2.12$) and some college ($b = -2.11$) also reach $p < .05$, but neither survives correction. The patterns differ by dimension, and outside a few contrasts the coefficients are modest. The three aspects---liking, listening, evaluating---are weakly coupled overall, yet their specific patterns of disagreement vary by the dimension and the demographic group.

But this seemingly weak overall social patterning masks an important distinction. Recall that the disagreement score $W_s(i)$ decomposes into two components (Equation~\ref{eq:genre}). The first is the \emph{genre-based} part $\sum_g \omega_s(i;g)$, which sums up how much a respondent's three aspects disagree within each of the twenty genres, and the \emph{cross-genre coherence} component $\gamma_s(i)$, which measures whether those per-genre disagreements reinforce or cancel each other across the full repertoire. To illustrate, a respondent might have high genre-based disagreement in rap (likes it, doesn't listen regularly, withholds status) and simultaneously in operatic music (doesn't like it, listens out of cultural obligation, grants status)---these work against each other in the total score when $\gamma_s(i)$ is negative, or together when it's positive. 

These two components of disagreement show different social patterns. The genre-based component is more socially structured, with demographics explaining $22.2\%$, $7.9\%$, $20.1\%$, and $2.9\%$ of its variation across the four dimensions (compared to $4.4\%$, $3.6\%$, $10.0\%$, and $1.9\%$ for the total scores). Upper-class respondents show elevated genre-based disagreement on the volume dimension, and race and ethnicity are linked to the genre-based component on the engagement-divide dimension. The cross-genre coherence component $\gamma_s(i)$---whether per-genre disagreements align or cancel---is more weakly structured overall, with $R^2$ values around $3.5\%$, $3.5\%$, $7.0\%$, and $1.8\%$ across the four dimensions. Social position thus shapes which genres anchor the genre-based component of disagreement, while coherence follows a weaker patterning of its own. Section~\ref{sec:coherence} examines the coherence component directly.

\subsection{Which Genres Anchor Complex Tastes? Demographic Concentration}
\label{sec:genre-specificity}

In Section~\ref{sec:social}, we found that demographics explain little of the total disagreement ($W_s$), yet the genre-based component $\sum_g \omega_s(i;g)$ shows more social structure. This raises a natural question. \emph{In which specific genres does demographic position shape disagreement?} The answer reveals that demographic concentration in complex tastes varies by both genre and dimension, and that social location channels disagreement into culturally meaningful objects.

Appendix~\ref{app:omega-genres} reports the correlations for all twenty genres (Figures~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d1}--\ref{fig:omega-genres-d4}). Every cell reports the Pearson correlation between a demographic variable and that genre's genre-based component $\omega_s(i;g)$. Each demographic variable enters as a 0/1 indicator---the four own-education categories, the four subjective-class identities, the six age groups, the six race and ethnicity categories, and the four income categories, plus parents' education, gender, and census region. Census region shows little genre-specific concentration anywhere in the taste space. Its largest correlation, gospel music among Southern respondents on the highbrow--popular dimension, is $|r| = 0.12$. Blue cells indicate positive correlations (higher disagreement in that demographic category); red cells indicate negative correlations. 

Which socio-demographic groups experience disagreement relative to which genres? We organize findings by the four dimensions.

\emph{On the highbrow--popular dimension}, age is associated with several patterns. Younger respondents (ages 18--29) hold more genre-based disagreement in the popular genres, including rap/hip-hop ($r = 0.31$), indie rock ($0.25$), and dance/club ($0.18$). The pattern reverses for older respondents, who show less disagreement in rap/hip-hop ($-0.22$ for ages 60--69, $-0.23$ for ages 70+) and indie rock ($-0.20$ for ages 70+), and more in big band ($0.26$ for ages 70+) and folk ($0.16$ for ages 70+). Race and ethnicity matter here as well. Hispanic respondents show elevated disagreement in Latin/salsa ($r = 0.44$), and White respondents show the mirror image in Latin/salsa ($-0.34$), rap/hip-hop ($-0.27$), and reggae ($-0.22$). Black respondents show elevated disagreement in gospel ($0.25$), blues ($0.23$), and rap/hip-hop ($0.20$). Postgraduate respondents show somewhat more disagreement in opera ($r = 0.17$).

\emph{On the volume dimension}, the same race and age contrasts appear in somewhat weaker form (Hispanic respondents in Latin/salsa, $r = 0.34$, against $-0.30$ for White respondents; younger respondents in indie rock, $0.13$, and older respondents in big band, $0.26$ for ages 70+), alongside an education gradient in the consecrated genres. Postgraduate respondents show elevated genre-based disagreement in opera ($r = 0.17$) and musicals ($0.15$), and respondents with college-educated parents show it in opera ($r = 0.15$), classical music ($r = 0.12$), and musicals ($r = 0.12$). Upper-class respondents show elevated disagreement in opera ($r = 0.15$), though their other correlations are small.

\emph{On the engagement-divide dimension}, the age and race patterns of the first dimension recur at nearly the same strength (rap/hip-hop $r = 0.31$ and indie rock $0.25$ for ages 18--29; Latin/salsa $0.43$ for Hispanic respondents against $-0.34$ for White; blues $0.26$ and rap/hip-hop $0.20$ for Black respondents). The overlap reflects the two dimensions' shared basis in liking and listening. The engagement-divide dimension nevertheless adds its own reading, since the disagreement it registers concentrates in the contrast between the diaspora genres and the guitar-rock cluster, the axis most closely linked to race and ethnicity (Section~\ref{sec:social}).

\emph{On the status-valuation dimension}, the associations are weak throughout, consistent with demographics explaining little of the variation in that component ($R^2 = 2.9\%$). The only correlation reaching $|r| = 0.15$ is postgraduate respondents in opera ($r = 0.18$); the next largest is parents' BA in opera ($0.14$).

The genre-based component thus becomes a window onto how demographic position works. It shapes not just whether people sit on the highbrow or popular side of the genre hierarchy (taste position), but \emph{where} and \emph{how} their aspects come apart (taste structure). Social location doesn't uniformly make people's aspects disagree more or less; instead, it directs that disagreement toward specific cultural objects. Demographics channel complex tastes through particular genres that carry social meaning and group identity.

Appendix~\ref{app:omega-genres} shows all twenty genres and all thirty demographic indicators, so the patterns can be checked where they hold and where they fade. Of the 2{,}400 correlations, 66 reach $|r| \ge 0.15$, and these cells are outlined in those figures. Demographics explain a larger share of the genre-based component than of the total score. That is consistent with demographics bearing more on where disagreement sits than on how much there is, but the design does not test this directly.

\subsection{The Social Patterning of Cross-Genre Coherence}
\label{sec:coherence}

The genre-based component is socially patterned. Age, race, education, and class channel disagreement into different genres. But what about the coherence component---the reinforcing or cancelling of per-genre disagreements across the full repertoire? 

We tested this with the same demographic variables and methods. Bivariate associations are tiny (Table~\ref{tab:coherence-eta}). Gender shows nothing anywhere. Only one association comes close to $\eta^2 = 0.05$---race/ethnicity on the engagement-divide dimension at $0.049$, which is also the dimension where race is most associated with the genres themselves. The total disagreement scores show the same pattern of small associations. Their largest bivariate association is also race on the engagement-divide dimension ($\eta^2 = 0.064$). Coherence, like aspect disagreement itself, is not the signature of any particular demographic group.

The joint regression models tell the same story with a little more structure. Demographics explain $3.5\%$ of the variation in $\gamma_1$ (highbrow--popular), $3.5\%$ in $\gamma_2$ (volume), $7.0\%$ in $\gamma_3$ (engagement divide), and $1.8\%$ in $\gamma_4$ (status)---weaker than the genre-based component's $22.2\%$, $7.9\%$, $20.1\%$, and $2.9\%$. The effects that do appear concentrate on $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_3$. Of the 96 coherence coefficients (Table~\ref{tab:coherence-regression}), 17 reach $p < .05$ unadjusted and 6 survive correction. The six survivors are Black respondents on $\gamma_3$, ages 40--49 and 50--59 on $\gamma_1$, college-educated parents on $\gamma_2$, and upper-class identity on $\gamma_2$ and $\gamma_4$. The postgraduate estimate on $\gamma_1$ and the Midwest and West estimates on $\gamma_3$ are unadjusted only, and some college and a bachelor's degree are negative on $\gamma_4$, also unadjusted. On the highbrow--popular dimension, coherence declines across the middle age cohorts ($b = -1.12$ at ages 50--59, $p < .001$), though the oldest cohort no longer differs from the youngest, and postgraduate respondents show somewhat more coherence ($b = 0.61$, $p < .05$). On the engagement-divide dimension, race stands out. Black respondents show higher coherence ($b = 1.43$, $p < .001$), as do respondents identifying with more than one race ($b = 0.99$, $p < .01$), while the Midwest and West show slightly lower coherence ($b = -0.40$ and $-0.55$, both $p < .05$). The volume dimension's few effects---coherence higher among respondents with college-educated parents ($b = 1.33$, $p < .001$) and among upper-class respondents---belong to the class story taken up below. The status-valuation dimension shows the least structure of all ($R^2 = 1.8\%$). Gender shows no significant coefficient on any dimension, and household income shows none after correction.

Because Equation~\ref{eq:genre} is an identity, and the coherence models use the same sample and predictors as the models for the total scores, every coefficient in Section~\ref{sec:social} splits exactly into a genre-based and a coherent part. This attribution sharpens the reading of the class and family-background results. The upper-class premium on the volume dimension ($W_2$, $b = 4.54$) is almost entirely coherence ($b = 4.09$), with only a small genre-based part ($b = 0.45$). In that sense the upper-class disagreement on the volume dimension looks more like a repertoire-wide alignment, with the same aspect displaced in the same direction across many genres, than like contradictions held in particular genres. The same total can arise from one genre held in intense contradiction or from many genres tilted the same way, and social position is associated with which form prevails. This association is descriptive and does not establish that social position causes either form.

Coherence is not always reinforcing. A considerable share of respondents show negative coherence, meaning their per-genre disagreements partially cancel and their total disagreement is smaller than the sum of its genre-level parts. About a third on the highbrow--popular dimension ($33\%$), a quarter on the volume dimension ($25\%$), and more than half on the engagement-divide dimension ($52\%$). One caveat concerns the status-valuation dimension. Evaluation is the only aspect that varies there, so a respondent who grants high status to many genres displaces their evaluation point in the same direction for every genre at once. For such respondents, much of what $\gamma_4$ records is this uniform displacement rather than configural contradiction, which is why $\gamma_4$ correlates with the magnitude of the global position ($r = 0.79$). Where coherence has social structure, then, it reflects these repertoire-wide orientations rather than localized contradiction. The genre-anchored form of complex taste---the kind whose social geography the previous section mapped---is the genre-based component's contribution.

\subsection{Genres as Targets of Complex Tastes}
\label{sec:duality}

Complex tastes have a dual structure. We've traced them from the individual perspective, asking \emph{who} has complex tastes and \emph{what} aspects disagree. But genres are targets too. Which genres attract complex tastes? The answer is that some genres generate much simpler responses than others.\footnote{At the genre level, we measure the proportion of respondents with simple tastes. These are the respondents whose three aspects all agree (either all yes---like, listen, grant status---or all no). The complement is the proportion with complex tastes in that genre (any mismatch across aspects).}

Heavy metal, Latin/salsa, and bluegrass produce largely simple tastes. Respectively, $70\%$, $67\%$, and $65\%$ of respondents respond consistently across all three aspects. You either like them and listen and value them, or you don't. Classical and opera are different. Only $33\%$ and $24\%$ of respondents respond simply to these genres. The rest hold them in contradiction. They might like classical music but rarely listen to it, or they listen out of cultural obligation while withholding judgments about the fans, or they think the music lacks status yet listen regularly. These prestige genres splinter audiences into complex configurations.

To answer this, we need a different analysis. The first MFA treated respondents as the units being analyzed and genres as variables. Now we flip that. Rows become genres and columns become respondent-responses (each respondent's yes/no on liking, listening, and evaluation for each genre). We re-run the MFA with genres as units. This is not simply a rearrangement of the original solution; it is a different analysis that asks new questions. In the original analysis, genres appeared only as variables; we could locate them through the composition of their audiences---the average profile of people who affirm them. But we cannot compute aspect-level agreement from the respondent analysis alone. Specifically, we cannot ask whether genres that are \emph{liked by many} are also \emph{listened to by many}---that is, whether the liking and listening audiences for each genre overlap. We also cannot see whether different aspects place individual genres in different positions. Both questions require treating genres as the units of analysis and respondents as the indicators.

Technically, this flip changes the analysis. Because MFA weights each block inversely to its separate analysis's strength in the first dimension, and transposing reshuffles which variables define the blocks, the balancing weights change. The transposed separate analyses yield different first eigenvalues ($\lambda_1' = 0.153/0.161/0.419$ for preference/consumption/evaluation respondent-indicators, versus the original $0.1550/0.1265/0.1942$ for genre-indicators). The transposed dimensions are thus optimized for spreading genres apart, not respondents. The key statistics we want---RV coefficients comparing aspects at the genre level, and aspect-specific partial points showing where different respondent-groups place each genre---do not exist in the respondent-level fit.\footnote{The transposed MFA was implemented by direct application of the algorithm in \citet{pages2014mfa} and validated by reproducing the respondent-level analysis. Eigenvalues, global and partial coordinates, RV coefficients, and group contributions are numerically consistent.}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig-genre-map-d12} \caption{Genre map from the transposed MFA (dimensions 1--2). Black points mark genre compromise positions. Colored points mark aspect partial points (segments connect each genre's compromise to its aspect-specific positions).}
\label{fig:genre-map-d12}
\end{figure}

From the genre perspective, the aspects \emph{agree} more. The RV coefficients jump to $0.92$ (preference and consumption nearly identical), $0.53$ (preference and evaluation), and $0.48$ (consumption and evaluation)---much higher than the individual-level $0.35$, $0.01$, and $0.02$. At the genre level, people who like a genre tend to listen to it and grant its fans high status. Genres that recruit likers recruit listeners too.

This is an aggregation result rather than a contradiction of the individual-level finding. The liking audience and the listening audience overlap for each genre. But the \emph{same individuals} don't always inhabit both groups. The person who likes opera but doesn't listen is in the liking audience; the person who listens but doesn't like is in the listening audience. Separately, they agree. Together, at the aggregate genre level, they agree. But at the individual level, people split apart. Complex tastes aren't something genres do; they're something individuals experience. Which individuals respond simply and which complexly varies person by person.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering \caption{Genre target profiles showing the percentage of respondents holding each genre in each of Ma's configurations ($N = 2{,}259$).}
\label{tab:genre-profile}
\input{tables/tab-genre-profile}
\end{table}

The transposed space has the following eigenvalues ($\lambda_1 = 2.25$, $14.8\%$ of the inertia; $\lambda_2 = 1.93$, $12.8\%$; $\lambda_3 = 1.25$, $8.2\%$; $\lambda_4 = 1.12$, $7.4\%$), with the first four dimensions accounting for $43.2\%$ of the total variation. The first two dimensions are shown in Figure~\ref{fig:genre-map-d12}, and the fourth dimension is shown in Figure~\ref{fig:genre-map-d14}. 

The first dimension opposes genres whose typical relation is status without engagement---classical ($+3.5$), opera ($+3.0$), and musicals ($+2.0$), with distant-praise rates correlating at $\rho = +0.84$ and taste-pose rates at $\rho = +0.59$---against genres most often held in the guilty pleasure ($\rho = -0.79$)\footnote{The correlation coefficients ($\rho$) reported throughout this section are Spearman rank correlations between each genre's coordinate on the transposed dimension and the genre-level prevalence (proportion of respondents, across all 2,259) who hold that genre in each of Ma's eight configuration types. For example, $\rho = +0.84$ for distant praise on Dimension 1 means that genres with high positive coordinates on that dimension tend to have high prevalence of distant-praise configurations, while genres with negative coordinates tend to have low prevalence of that configuration.} and distanced consumption ($-0.82$) configurations. These last include top 40 ($-2.1$), rap/hip-hop ($-1.6$), classic rock/oldies ($-1.6$), and contemporary rock ($-1.4$)---familiar genres most often held with engaged disagreement. This dimension, in plain terms, measures the \emph{engagement--detachment} contrast at the genre level. On the positive side sit prestige genres whose audiences are defined partly by abstention from engagement (the listener who values classical music highly but rarely listens), while the negative side includes genres where respondents' disagreement arises from active engagement despite reservations about status (the guilty-pleasure listener who loves the genre but withholds attributing high status to the genre's audience). In effect, this dimension answers the question of whether a genre recruits audiences through engagement or through distant admiration.

The second dimension is a \emph{configuration axis}. Genres are ordered by the complex-taste profiles they attract (Table~\ref{tab:genre-profile}; Figure~\ref{fig:genre-map-d12}). At the positive pole sit the genres most often held in simple non-taste ($\rho = +0.80$)---rap/hip-hop ($+1.7$), reggae ($+1.5$), Latin/salsa ($+1.4$), and heavy metal ($+1.3$). At the negative pole sit the genres respondents actively hold---in simple positive taste ($\rho = -0.81$), as taste poses ($-0.59$), as guilty pleasures ($-0.43$), or as justified abstentions ($-0.40$)---led by classic rock/oldies ($-3.5$), mood/easy listening ($-2.1$), and country ($-1.7$). Opera ($+1.0$) is a partial exception. Its characteristic configuration is distant praise (with $58.9\%$ of respondents holding it in that configuration), yet its coordinate sits on the non-taste side, alongside a low consumption rate ($8.5\%$). The duality is asymmetric in the way complex-taste theory anticipates. The prototypical guilty-pleasure genres are among the least credited with high status (evaluation rates of $8$--$14\%$ for classic rock/oldies, country, and top 40), and the prototypical distant-praise genre is among the least consumed ($8.5\%$ for opera, against $8.2\%$ for bluegrass).

The partial points reveal how audiences for the same genre diverge by aspect. Like in our original MFA analysis focused on individuals, in the transposed MFA, each genre has three partial coordinates per dimension. One is for the preference-audience (respondents who like it), one for the consumption-audience (respondents who listen), and one for the evaluation-audience (respondents who grant it high status). When these three points cluster together, a genre recruits the same people across all three aspects---likers and listeners and status-granters occupy the same region. When they spread far apart, a genre's audiences are segmented. The people who like it are positioned differently from those who listen to it or who value its fans highly. The configuration axis (Dimension 2 of Figure~\ref{fig:genre-map-d12}) shows this segmentation most directly. Rap/hip-hop illustrates the pattern on the simple-non-taste pole. Its liking and listening audiences sit at $+2.8$ and $+1.9$, while its evaluation audience sits at $+0.4$. Classic rock/oldies shows the opposite arrangement, with liking and listening audiences far on the other side ($-4.8$ and $-5.5$) and status-granters near the middle ($-0.2$). Opera splits across the origin, with preference and consumption on the simple-non-taste side ($+2.2$ and $+1.4$) and evaluation on the other side ($-0.7$). In each case, the people who grant a genre high status occupy a different position on this axis from the people who like or listen to it. 

More broadly, three patterns emerge. Opera has the widest spread across its three partial points on the status-without-engagement dimension (3.1 points), where its status-granting audience sits even further toward the prestige pole ($+4.9$) than its liking and listening audiences do ($+2.5$ and $+1.8$). Classic rock/oldies has the widest spread on the configuration axis (5.3 points). Its liking and listening audiences sit at $-4.8$ and $-5.5$, while its status-granting audience sits near the middle ($-0.2$). Most other genres recruit relatively unified audiences where the same people like, listen, and evaluate, or where segmentation concentrates on a single dimension rather than cutting across multiple ways of relating to the music.

The fourth dimension orders genres by the racial composition of their audiences. Blues/R\&B ($+2.7$ and $+2.5$ for its liking and listening partial points), jazz ($+2.4$ and $+1.9$), and rap/hip-hop ($+1.1$ and $+1.8$) sit at the positive pole, and Black respondents make up $19\%$, $16\%$, and $23\%$ of their liking audiences, against $12\%$ of the sample. Gospel and reggae also sit high ($+0.7$ and $+0.5$), with Black shares of $23\%$ and $21\%$. At the negative pole sit heavy metal ($-2.5$ and $-1.7$), country ($-2.0$ and $-3.0$), indie rock, bluegrass, and folk, whose liking audiences are $6$--$9\%$ Black. Across the twenty genres, a genre's coordinate correlates at $r = 0.75$ with the Black share of its liking audience (95\% CI $0.46$ to $0.90$), and dropping any single genre leaves the correlation between $0.73$ and $0.79$. Controlling for each genre's liking rate (the proportion of respondents who like it), the partial correlation is $0.78$ (95\% CI $0.51$ to $0.91$; permutation $p < .001$). The white share shows the mirror pattern (partial $r = -0.63$, 95\% CI $-0.84$ to $-0.25$), but the two shares are related ($r = -0.77$). In a joint model with the liking rate, the Black share is the only one of the two shares that remains significant ($b = 14.8$, SE $4.9$, $p = .008$), and the white share adds nothing once the Black share is included ($b = -0.47$, $p = .87$). The Hispanic share correlates at $0.15$ in raw terms. The female share of liking audiences correlates at $0.39$ in raw terms, but this association does not survive controls (partial $r = 0.37$ given the liking rate, 95\% CI $-0.10$ to $0.70$; partial $r = -0.18$ given the Black share).\footnote{Controlling for each genre's listening rate instead of its liking rate gives a partial correlation of $0.75$ for the Black share (95\% CI $0.44$ to $0.90$; permutation $p < .001$) and $-0.54$ for the white share (95\% CI $-0.80$ to $-0.11$; permutation $p = .014$). Rank-based partial correlations controlling for liking rate are $0.84$ for the Black share and $-0.69$ for the white share. Confidence intervals use the Fisher $z$ transformation with standard error $1/\sqrt{n-4}$, and permutation $p$-values come from 10{,}000 shuffles of the residualized audience shares.} Evaluation contributes only $7\%$ of this axis, and its partial coordinates span roughly $\pm0.6$ against roughly $\pm3$ for liking and listening, so the dimension describes who likes and listens to genres rather than who grants them status. Mood/easy listening also has a positive coordinate but a near-average Black liking audience ($13\%$), so race does not explain its position. Because these are correlations across twenty genres, they describe which genres have racially distinct audiences; they do not show how individual respondents' race relates to their genre positions. Each genre's coordinate is also computed from the liking patterns of the same respondents whose race is tabulated by genre, so part of the correlation with the Black share of liking audiences is built into the construction. A split-sample check, computing the coordinates on one random half of respondents and correlating them with audience shares from the other half, would address this for the liking audience. We have not run it. The individual-level engagement divide (Dimension 3) is also racially patterned. Race has the largest bivariate association with its disagreement score ($\eta^2 = 0.064$; Table~\ref{tab:w-eta}), so the two axes may share a racial basis, although we have not verified that they are the same dimension at the two levels.
