Colored points mark aspect partial points (segments connect each genre's compromise to its aspect-specific positions). The fourth dimension orders genres by the Black share of their liking audiences, from genres with above-average Black representation (Blues/R\&B, jazz, rap/hip-hop) to genres with below-average representation (country, heavy metal, bluegrass, folk).}
\label{fig:genre-map-d14}
\end{figure}

\section{Discussion}

This paper has pursued a geometric approach to measuring complex tastes---the misalignments between preference, consumption, and evaluation in cultural fields. The results support three core findings about musical taste in contemporary America.

\emph{First, the three aspects are empirically independent.} Preference and consumption correlate moderately (RV = 0.35), but evaluation is nearly orthogonal to both (RV = 0.01). This independence is the geometric signature of the complex-taste concept. If all three were measuring the same underlying thing, we could ignore two of them. But they don't. What you like, what you listen to, and what you praise are three separable judgments that follow different logics.

\emph{Second, the shared structure spans more than two dimensions.} Dimensions 1 and 2 carry $15.5\%$ of the inertia, and Dimensions 3 and 4 carry another $10.5\%$. Dimension 1 is the classical highbrow--popular hierarchy. Dimension 2 is volume, the number of genres someone likes and listens to. Dimension 3 is the engagement divide, which is racially patterned at the individual level. Dimension 4 is status valuation, where preference and consumption contribute $4.3\%$ and $4.6\%$ and evaluation carries most of the dimension.

\emph{Third, complex tastes are common in these data.} The disagreement scores ($W_s$) account for $49\%$, $55\%$, $52\%$, and $66\%$ of the average respondent's variation on the four dimensions. Combinatorially, the average respondent holds $10.2$ of $20$ genres in complex configurations. Only 12 respondents (of 2,259) hold no complex configuration at all. Under Ma's classification, almost every respondent holds at least one complex configuration. The classification counts a genre as complex whenever any aspect departs from the others, so part of this prevalence follows from the definition.

Total disagreement is only weakly associated with demographics. Where respondents sit on the highbrow--popular hierarchy has long been linked to age, education, and class \citep{lizardo2015musical-8c6}. Demographics explain little of total disagreement ($R^2 = 1.9$ to $10.0\%$). Gender illustrates the point. No coefficient for women reaches significance in the models for the four disagreement scores or their coherence components, and gender accounts for less than one percent of the variation in each. The dispersion that makes a person's taste complex is only weakly associated with the social positions that sort people by consumption patterns. The genre-based component is associated with more variation (up to $22\%$), so this claim applies to total disagreement rather than to every component of it. This fits the individual-level theory. The independence of the aspects at the population level generates disagreement at the individual level whenever people don't occupy all three positions simultaneously.

Finally, the duality shows that from the genre perspective the aspects agree. Liking, listening, and evaluation audiences overlap. Across genres, the Black share of liking audiences tracks the fourth transposed dimension (partial $r = 0.78$ controlling for each genre's liking rate). The female share of liking audiences also correlates with that dimension in raw terms ($r = 0.39$), but this association does not survive controlling for the Black share (partial $r = -0.18$), because the two audience shares are themselves correlated ($r = 0.57$). With twenty genres these are descriptive associations, not tests of individual-level effects. But because individuals don't equally participate in all three audiences, complex tastes emerge. A person may be an opera enthusiast (likes, listens, praises), an uninterested person (none of the above), or any combination. The six complex configurations differ in frequency. Justified abstention, guilty pleasure, and distant praise each average more than two genres per respondent, while distanced consumption ($0.4$) and pre-acquired taste ($0.1$) are rare in this sample.

Future work might explore whether these patterns generalize to other cultural fields---visual art, film, fashion---or whether music has distinctive properties. The geometric approach allows measurement of the degree to which cultural judgment is unified or fragmented. The results here suggest that judgment in this field appears more fragmented than a single taste dimension would imply. This rests on one survey and twenty genres.

\subsection{Limitations}

The data come from one 2012 online survey of U.S. adults, and the analysis is unweighted. The results therefore describe this sample rather than the population. Unfamiliarity is coded as non-liking, following the preference measure. A respondent who has never heard of a genre thus counts the same as one who dislikes it, so preference prevalence partly reflects familiarity. Evaluation is a constructed binary, and its coding rule is a judgment call. The 412 respondents (18\% of the 2,259) who are constant within a block enter as supplementary individuals rather than as active respondents, and refitting with them as active yields matched dimensions with correlations of 0.87 to 0.97. The transposed results rest on twenty genres, so the cross-genre correlations have few effective observations, and the transposed coordinates are computed from the same respondents whose race is tabulated by genre. The regression models are cross-sectional and descriptive, and their outcomes are right-skewed. The log-outcome models agree on the upper-class effects but not on every age coefficient.

\section{Comparison of the Geometric and Discrete Approach}
\label{app:comparison}

\subsection{Comparing the Two Measures}
\label{sec:antinomies}

The geometric score is one way to capture complex tastes, and Ma's configurations offer another. The two mostly do not coincide. The configuration count correlates only weakly with $W_s(i)$, and the weakness comes mainly from coherence, the cross-genre part of $W_s(i)$. Ma's framework works genre by genre. It classifies a person's preference, engagement, and evaluation of each genre into one of eight configurations. Two of these have the three aspects agreeing, and six have them diverging, such as guilty pleasures, taste poses, and distanced consumption (Appendix~\ref{app:configurations} defines them). Counting how many of a person's 20 genres fall into the six complex configurations gives their total count of complex tastes, the number of genres in which they hold one of these six configurations.

Most of $W_s(i)$ is coherence. It makes up 85--89\% of the variance in $W_s(i)$ on each dimension, and the configuration counts correlate only weakly with it (all $|\rho| \le 0.22$). The genre-based component behaves differently. The total count correlates with it at 0.61, 0.58, 0.63, and 0.24 across the four dimensions, against 0.17, 0.28, 0.18, and $-0.11$ for $W_s(i)$. A plausible reason is that coherence is a cross-genre term, while the count classifies each genre separately. The total count also correlates with the global coordinates, at $0.66$ on the volume dimension and $-0.40$ on the highbrow--popular dimension.

Figure~\ref{fig:signatures} shows how each configuration count correlates with four geometric measures on each dimension. The four measures are the global coordinate, the aspect-disagreement score, its genre-based component, and its coherence component. The configuration types differ in their signatures. Distant praise and taste poses correlate positively with the status-valuation coordinate ($\rho = 0.69$ and $0.42$), guilty pleasures correlate negatively with it ($\rho = -0.40$), and guilty pleasures correlate with the genre-based components on the highbrow--popular and engagement-divide dimensions ($\rho = 0.50$ and $0.47$). These are point estimates from Spearman correlations among $N = 2{,}259$ respondents, with no confidence intervals, so differences of a few hundredths should not be read as meaningful.

Configurations are also heterogeneous internally. Among respondents with guilty pleasures, the status-valuation score $W_4$ has a mean of $4.5$ and an SD of $10.4$, so the same configuration spans different degrees of disagreement, depending on which genres hold it and how much the aspects disagree within them.\footnote{Figure~\ref{fig:config-variation} visualizes the full range of within-configuration variation across all eight configurations and four dimensions.}

Heatmap shows Spearman correlations between configuration counts (per respondent, out of 20 genres) and MFA coordinates and complex-taste scores ($N = 2{,}259$), across four dimensions and four score types (global coordinates, aspect-disagreement, its genre-based component, and its coherence component).}
\label{fig:signatures}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Within-Configuration Variation in Disagreement Scores}
\label{app:config-variation}

Respondents classified into the same configuration type show variation in their aspect-disagreement scores across all four dimensions. Figure~\ref{fig:config-variation} displays the mean and standard deviation of $W_s$ for each configuration, revealing that the overlap in disagreement levels both within and across configuration types suggests why the correlation between the geometric and combinatorial measures is weak. One plausible reason is that the same configuration can span different numbers of genres and different internal structures, so respondents who share a configuration can differ in $W_s$. Figure~\ref{fig:config-variation} shows the variation but does not decompose it, so this explanation is a hypothesis. The disagreement associated with a particular configuration depends not just on its presence, but on how spread out across the genre space it becomes.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig-config-variation} \caption{Aspect-disagreement scores by configuration type. Bars show the mean $W_s$ for each of Ma's eight configurations on each of the four dimensions; error bars show $\pm 1$ SD. The overlap both within and across configuration types is consistent with the weak correlation between configuration counts and geometric disagreement scores.}
\label{fig:config-variation}
\end{figure}

\section{The Combinatorial Measure and Ma's Eight Configurations}
\label{app:configurations}

The geometric measure locates complex tastes continuously in the common space. As a discrete complement, each genre--respondent pair can be classified into one of Ma's eight configurations from the binary triple of orientations (preference, consumption, evaluation). Two of the eight are simple, namely the simple taste $(+++)$ and the simple non-taste $(---)$, and six are complex.

Under this classification, complex configurations are the common case. Figure~\ref{fig:configurations} reports the mean number of genres held in each configuration. The average respondent holds $10.2$ of the $20$ genres in a complex configuration, and only $12$ of $2{,}259$ respondents hold no complex configuration at all. The most frequent complex configuration is the \emph{justified abstention} ($3.3$ genres on average), followed by the \emph{guilty pleasure} ($3.2$) and \emph{distant praise} ($2.2$). Respondents often like genres whose fans they don't credit with high status, grant high status to genres they neither like nor consume, and like-and-consume genres whose fans they don't think of as high status. The taste pose ($1.0$) and the rare variants---distanced consumption ($0.4$) and the pre-acquired taste ($0.1$)---are comparatively infrequent, while the simple non-taste ($8.9$) is the single largest configuration. These results describe this survey and this classification, not an established population norm.

\section{Genre-Specific Disagreement Across All Twenty Genres}
\label{app:omega-genres}

Figures~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d1}--\ref{fig:omega-genres-d4} show the genre-by-demographic matrices for all twenty genres, one figure per dimension. Each cell reports the Pearson correlation between a demographic variable (rows) and the genre-based component $\omega_s(i;g)$ of the genre named in the column. All thirty demographic indicators are shown. They include the four own-education categories (high school or less, some college, bachelor's, postgraduate), parents' education, the four subjective-class identities (lower, working, middle, upper), gender, the six age groups, the six race and ethnicity categories (White, Black, Hispanic, Asian, Multirace, Other), the four income categories, and the four census regions. The encoding is as described in Section~\ref{sec:genre-specificity}; blue cells are positive, red cells negative, and every value is printed.

The matrices show which genres carry the demographic patterning. On the highbrow--popular dimension (Figure~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d1}) the age gradient appears in the popular block (rap/hip-hop $0.31$, indie rock $0.25$, and dance/club $0.18$ for ages 18--29, against $-0.23$ for rap/hip-hop at ages 70+), the race indicators peak in Latin/salsa (Hispanic respondents $0.44$, White $-0.34$), and Black respondents show elevated disagreement in gospel ($0.25$) and blues ($0.23$). On the volume dimension (Figure~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d2}) the education contrasts appear (postgraduate respondents $0.17$ for opera and $0.15$ for musicals, parents' education $0.15$ for opera and $0.12$ for classical music and musicals) alongside the race contrasts in the diaspora genres (Hispanic respondents $0.34$ for Latin/salsa, Black respondents $0.20$ for gospel and $0.18$ for reggae). On the engagement-divide dimension (Figure~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d3}) the first dimension's age and race patterns recur at nearly full strength (rap/hip-hop $0.31$ for ages 18--29; Latin/salsa $0.43$ for Hispanic respondents against $-0.34$ for White). On the status-valuation dimension (Figure~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d4}) the associations are weak throughout; the largest is postgraduate respondents in opera ($0.18$).
